title: More than 1 in 10 addresses used as holiday homes in some areas of England and Wales
meta_description: Our analysis of Census 2021 data reveals the hotspots where second addresses are used as holiday homes across England and Wales. Explore these locations, how many people use them and where they travel from

breadcrumb.text: More than 1 in 10 addresses used as holiday homes in some areas of England and Wales

lede: Our analysis of Census 2021 data reveals the hotspots where second addresses are used as holiday homes across England and Wales. Explore these locations, how many people use them and where they travel from

body.text: 20 June 2023
[This page is also available in Welsh (Cymraeg)](https://cy.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/morethan1in10addressesusedasholidayhomesinsomeareasofenglandandwales/2023-06-20).
Around 70,000 second addresses were used as holiday homes, visited by more than 200,000 people in England and Wales, according to Census 2021.

Holiday homes accounted for 4.1% of all second addresses and were mainly concentrated in coastal areas, Areas of Outstanding Natural Beauty or national parks, including the Lake District, Dartmoor and Eryri (Snowdonia).

Census 2021 data on second addresses only include people who usually reside in England and Wales who said they spend at least 30 days a year at the address. The total number of second addresses used as holiday homes, and people who use them, are likely to be higher.
There may have been an impact on these data from the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, but these are difficult to measure.
The popular holiday destination of Cornwall had the highest numbers of holiday homes and people who use them, with 6,080 holiday homes and 14,230 holiday home users.

As a proportion of the local housing supply (all dwellings excluding communal establishments), South Hams on the coast of Devon and Gwynedd in North Wales had the highest proportions of holiday homes. In some smaller areas, more than 1 in 10 addresses were being used as holiday homes.
And when adjusting for the local population, Gwynedd and the Isle of Anglesey in North Wales saw the highest proportions of holiday home users travelling to their areas.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: The South West had the highest concentration of holiday homes compared with other English regions and Wales, at 7.5 for every 1,000 homes.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: This was followed by Wales, with 6.9 holiday homes for every 1,000 homes. London had the lowest, at 0.6 per 1,000.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: The figure was higher in local authority areas known as popular tourist destinations. In South Hams in Devon, there were 44.1 holiday homes for every 1,000 homes.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: This was the highest rate of any local authority area in England and Wales excluding the Isles of Scilly, which has a particularly small resident population.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: South Hams has a long coastline and is home to the southern part of Dartmoor National Park, as well as the South Devon Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: South Hams was followed by Gwynedd in North Wales (41.0 per 1,000 homes), which contains most of Eryri (Snowdonia) National Park, North Norfolk (38.7 per 1,000) and the Isle of Anglesey (32.9 per 1,000).

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: Within local authorities, there were some areas where the concentration of holiday homes was even higher.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: The following areas are known as Middle layer Super Output Areas (MSOAs), which comprise of between 2,000 and 6,000 households. We use [names for them created by the House of Commons Library](https://houseofcommonslibrary.github.io/msoanames/).

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.text: In the Salcombe, Malborough and Thurlestone area of South Hams, there were 171.9 holiday homes for every 1,000 homes. In Abersoch and Aberdaron in Gwynedd, the figure was 153.3 per 1,000.

body.text: Both the UK and Welsh parliaments have recently passed new laws to further regulate the ownership of second homes.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.h3: Holiday home hotspots
body.h4: Location of second addresses used as a holiday home, by Middle layer Super Output Area, England and Wales
body.text: Last year, the [UK Government changed the law](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/gove-closes-tax-loophole-on-second-homes) so that second homeowners would pay council tax on properties that are not genuine holiday lets. Second homeowners must now prove holiday lets are rented out for a minimum of 70 days a year, and are available to rent for at least 140 days.

body.h2: The South West of England and Wales are holiday home hotspots
body.h3: Holiday home hotspots
body.h4: Location of second addresses used as a holiday home, by Middle layer Super Output Area, England and Wales
body.text: The Welsh Government recently [increased its own letting requirements](https://www.gov.wales/new-tax-rules-second-homes) so properties must be rented out for at least 182 days a year, and available for at least 252 days. It has also raised the maximum council tax premium that councils can apply to second homes, to up to four times the standard rate.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Almost half (48.5%) of those who used a second address as a holiday home travelled within the UK, up from 42.3% in the 2011 Census.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Around 4 in 10 (41.8%) of those who used holiday homes in the UK travelled less than 100 kilometres (km) from their usual address, as shown in our [Characteristics of people in England and Wales with a second address: Census 2021](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/housing/articles/characteristicsofpeopleinenglandandwaleswithasecondaddress/census2021) article.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: And around 1 in every 50 (1.9%) people who used a holiday home stayed in the same local authority as their usual residence.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: At a regional level, using holiday homes in the same area as a usual residence was most common in Yorkshire and the North of England.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Around two-thirds of holiday home users in these areas came from within the same region, 63.5% in Yorkshire and the Humber, 63.2% in the North East, and 61.7% in the North West.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Of the 93,650 Londoners who used second addresses as holiday homes, almost a quarter travelled within the South of England, with 14.4% going to the South East, and 10.0% to the South West.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Almost two-thirds (62.3%) of Londoners who used holiday homes travelled outside of the UK, the highest proportion of any region of England, or Wales. Only 0.7% stayed at addresses in London.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Holiday home users from London were least likely to go to the North East of England (0.3%) or Northern Ireland (0.2%).

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Wales was the most common destination inside the UK for people from the:

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: West Midlands, where 22.4% of people who used a second address as a holiday home travelled to Wales.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: North West, where 22.2% of all holiday home users travelled to Wales.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: 20,045 people from these areas travelled to Wales, accounting for more than half of the 36,370 people who used holiday homes in Wales.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Among all people from Wales who used a second address as a holiday home, more than half (53.8%) travelled to addresses within the country.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Slightly over a third (34.0%) travelled outside the UK, which was the lowest proportion of holiday home users who travelled abroad, compared with English regions.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Around 1 in 10 (11.3%) of Welsh holiday home users travelled to England. This was just under 2,000 people, more than half of whom used addresses in the South West.

body.h2: Holidaying in the UK becoming more common
body.text: Travelling in the other direction across the border between England and Wales, 26,940 people from England used second addresses in Wales as holiday homes. However, this was a lower proportion of all English holiday homes users travelling to Wales (6.3%) than the proportion of Welsh holiday home users travelling to England (11.3%).

body.text: A total of 36,370 people were using holiday homes in Wales, equivalent to 11.7 holiday home users for every 1,000 local residents.

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: While more people said they used second addresses as holiday homes in the South West of England (48,075), this was equal to 8.4 people per 1,000 local residents.

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: The local authority with the highest proportion of holiday home users relative to its population was Gwynedd in North Wales.

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: For every 1,000 local residents, 79.0 people from other local authorities used a holiday home in the area (9,270 people in total).

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: More than three-quarters of people who used holiday homes in Gwynedd came from England’s North West (43.3%) or West Midlands (32.1%).

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: There is a similar situation in the Isle of Anglesey, which was the second most popular holiday home destination in England and Wales.

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: A total of 63.3 people per 1,000 local residents (4,375 people) came to holiday homes in the area from another local authority.

body.h2: Holiday home use increasing in North Wales hotspots
body.text: Anglesey also saw the largest increase in the number of holiday home users of any local authority in England and Wales, up from 41.5 per 1,000 in 2011.

body.h3: Kensington and Chelsea had the highest proportion of residents who used second addresses as holiday homes
body.h4: Percentage of usual residents who used a second address as a holiday home, Census 2021
body.text: Among those from Waverley, 6.5% travelled to Cornwall, 5.5% to Dorset, and 4.5% to the Isle of Wight.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: Holiday homes most likely to be detached

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: In addition to location, we can look at the number of bedrooms and accommodation type of second addresses used as holiday homes.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: Information on accommodation type could be identified for 85.6% of all holiday homes in our data, and the number of bedrooms was available for 81.0%.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: Across England and Wales, holiday homes were most likely to be detached (33.0%), while semi-detached houses were the most common property type for all homes recorded in Census 2021. In Wales, 44.8% of holiday homes were detached properties.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: Caravans or other mobile or temporary structures made up 5.9% of holiday homes across England and Wales. Although 50.8% of holiday homes in East Lindsey were caravans or other mobile temporary structures, they made up less than 10% of holiday homes in the 19 other areas where holiday homes were most common.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: The most common number of bedrooms for holiday homes across England was two (40.0%), followed by three (32.3%).

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: In Wales, three-bedroom holiday homes were most common (37.9%), while two-bedroom properties made up 36.5%.

body.h2: Holiday homes most likely to be detached
body.text: More figures on holiday homes by number of bedrooms and accommodation type, and other types of second addresses including parent or guardian or students' home addresses, can be found in our data downloads.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: About the data

body.h2: About the data
body.text: These data only include people who usually reside in England and Wales who said they spend at least 30 days a year at a second address.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: People that are not usual residents in England and Wales may have a second address in England and Wales but would not be captured in these data.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: Some second addresses may not be used by any usual residents in England and Wales for at least 30 days a year, and these would not be captured in these data.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: For Census 2021, a usual resident of the UK is anyone who, on Census Day, was in the UK and had stayed or intended to stay in the UK for a period of 12 months or more, or had a permanent UK address and was outside the UK and intended to be outside the UK for less than 12 months.

body.h2: About the data
body.text: Data on number of bedrooms and accommodation type of the second address is taken from Valuation Office Agency (VOA) Property Attributes data, or Census 2021 data if available. It is not possible to get this information for all dwellings we have listed as second addresses.
